utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties would like to raise a preliminary matter. The Prosecution first. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Lubura is scheduled to testify this week and he is the first witness where we have formally made an application to tender his Karadzic cross through 98 and 92 bis. I was just wondering whether -- Mr. Jeremy is here to answer any particular question the Chamber might have regarding this particular witness and I'm certainly available to answer any questions in general about the proposal, but it would be helpful, I think, not only for us but probably for everyone involved in the trial to have an indication of how we might best prepare for this examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. As a matter of fact, it was on our agenda as well. We are considering how to proceed because you made proposals on the 19th of May on the tendering of -- tendering of portions of transcripts, and I think we have no definite answer yet. We are still considering it. So if you would -- we'll try to speed that up so that you are in a position that you know what to expect, when it comes to Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And related to that, Your Honour, if perhaps we could have just some clarification about the witness order for the week. I think there is some uncertainty in our mind about who the next witness is after Mr. Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we will continue with Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I discussed the same issue with Mr. Jeremy and Mr. Groome. Mr. Cvoro is a bit longer witness, I think, and we have to finish Mr. Lubura on Tuesday, so we were thinking maybe it's wiser to start Mr. Lubura immediately after Mr. Lalovic. But I forgot to mention that on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because then it was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About Mr. Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I think reference was made to it once on the Monday and the Tuesday, that's -- I have a recollection of that. But it was not very explicit last Friday. Then this means that it's even more urgent that we deal with the issue of -- of the evidence of Mr. Lubura, and we'll give it priority at this same morning still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just we did not anticipate -- we anticipate the earliest possible time we would have to cross-examine Mr. Lubura was tomorrow, so we wouldn't be prepared to go forward with the cross. But I think if we proceed this way, it's unlikely that we would get to the cross anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Lukic, you -- I think it was clear that the Defence opposed the -- the proposals made by the Prosecution. Is there anything you'd like to add to that in -- apart from what you told us already in court. I think you compared it with what happened during the Prosecution's case and that you never did it, whether true or not, I think that was then contradicted by the -- by the Prosecution. Is there anything you'd like to add to what you said last time on the matter. Not to repeat it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just asked for Mr. Ivetic to be with us since he was dealing with that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just perhaps some helpful information. I'm not sure whether -- the Chamber doesn't seem to be aware that there was a filing filed by the Defence last week. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact there was, and that was on my agenda. As a matter of fact, that on my agenda was an announcement that if we would not have yet determined what to do with your proposals that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I should not make any further filings. That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was on my agenda [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to make sure that you were aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, we are aware of that. And then if you would like to add anything, Mr. Lukic, you should do it at the beginning of the next session, because we are now urgently seized of the matter and especially since the witness may already start his testimony later today, then we don't have much time, and we would not like to leave Mr. Jeremy without any guidance. Nothing else. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I have one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours we saw these days that our witnesses are cross-examined on the issue whether they talk to each other or do not talk to each other. I can inform you that apart from the VWS Section, we warn our witnesses not to talk with each other about the case. The fact is that they are usually placed in the same hotel as a group, so they do so socialise with each other. They claim to us that they do not talk about that -- the case. The only one who told us that he discussed the case with another witness was Mr. Maletic, and we instructed him to report that to the Chamber. So we are uncertain how to proceed on this issue. Should the witnesses be placed in different hotels; should they be told not to speak to each other at all; or should they be told to talk about the case? I see all Your Honours disagreeing with my last proposal and I that I we all agree on that. But we -- we do not know how to convince both Your Honours and the Prosecution that they do not talk about the case. We would rather have some guidance how to prevent any suspicion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, to prevent suspicion always depends on the factual circumstances. We'll consider that. Now, if are you not in the same hotel but if you were on the same flight, then it may not always be very effective, and it -- I think it's rather natural that if you come to The Hague to testify that there's an inclination to speak about the purpose for which you came to The Hague, whether it's in general terms or whether that's in more specific terms. Therefore, we'll -- we'll consider it, what to do -- let me leave it to that. We'll consider whether we'll give you any guidance or not. We'll further discuss the matter and -- At the same time, I think that witnesses are bound not to speak about the case once they've -- once they've taken the stand and we always instruct them not that. Even there whether that instruction is always followed, one never knows. But in itself, to say, You cannot speak to someone else, that, of course, is not easy, that people could not have conversations privately on matters if they come from the same area or if they want to exchange their views on how nice The Hague is that's, of course, something the Chamber is not -- we're not mastering the personal relations of witnesses. But we'll consider it further. But certainly at this moment there's no instruction for the witnesses to talk about the case. They might even do it without such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, if I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- what I noticed that after the witness starts with his testimony, I noticed that he is not socialising at all with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Especially with us. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No they -- of course, you shouldn't even come close those witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- once they have taken the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we enter the hallway, for example, in the hotel, and he would be standing somewhere in the hallway. He would return immediately and leave. And I would see that is he not in the same company with others when we enter the hallway of the hotel. So after -- after he starts his testimony, I'm sure that they don't have any kind of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least if I take it purely from a factual point of view, then you can affirm that, as long as they are within your sight, they are not seeking any contact with you, and they're not socialising with others. What happens after they have turned, we do not know, you do not know. Just from a factual point of view, I leave it to that, and it strengthens your conviction that they are abiding what they are supposed to do. That's how I understand your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to try to refer to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. We'll consider whether or not any further instruction -- any further guidance will be given. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Nothing else? Then if the Defence is ready to call its next witness, no protective measures, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could Mr. Lalovic be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lalovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Lalovic. Mr. Lalovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic, and you'll find him to your left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all -- actually, let us call up 1D1650. That should be the statement of General Lalovic. Do you see it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The signature at the bottom, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at the last page now. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at the previous page, please, in both versions. Let us please focus on paragraph 28. The Defence is going to ask for this paragraph to be deleted from the statement and I'm going to explain why. I showed Mr. Lalovic this document on the computer screen, and it had to be zoomed in 400 per cent, in order to see what is written there. We all know that the print is very fine on this chart. However, here, in The Hague, when we looked at it very carefully, Mr. Lalovic realised that he is marked on that chart as the commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade, and the impression that we both had when we watched it in the electronic version was that General Lalovic was shown as part of the Main Staff in 1995. So now we're going to ask for this paragraph 28 to be excluded from the statement altogether because the organisational chart is correct in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to say that would it be more appropriate for General Lalovic to give his assessment of the chart and -- I mean, that's the evidence that's being led rather than Mr. Lukic recounting the evidence from a conversation over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, it's Mr. Lukic who can propose not to tender part of this statement. That is, I would say -- and if you strike it when -- I take it that you'll -- or it's just the last line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we'll strike the whole the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You strike the whole of the paragraph. Then you're invited to upload a new version. And, Mr. Lalovic, your statement would not be any less true if we take out paragraph 28, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is that -- that resolves the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you're invited to upload a new version. We have now on the transcript that the witness signed this complete version but that the witness says that striking paragraph 28 doesn't make it any less true for the remaining paragraphs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we have one more correction but only in English version, and I was kindly warned by Mr. Groome this morning that there is mistake in the translation of one number. In -- in English version, we need paragraph 19. In both versions. In the fourth line of paragraph 19, in English version, we can see a date, 6th of April, 1993. And it should read 1996, 6th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you don't even need to be a trained translator to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's not logical the way it was now written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing -- matter is then whether it's inconsistent whether 1993 or 1996 is the right date is still to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, please take a look at paragraph 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It cannot be 1993 or 1995 would be wrong. That's another possibility, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this sentence in paragraph 19: "From the 26th of May 1995 to" what should is say there? The 6th of April of, what, 1996, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. 1996, I served as the chief of military police affairs at the security department of the Herzegovina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement corrected in this way, does it faithfully portray what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you said to me, you talked to me; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you basically respond in the same way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement as well the associated documents and we would like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not object to the admission of the statement. However, we would seek to -- to -- to discuss and make submissions on the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start then with the statement itself. Madam Registrar, the statement would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1650 receives number D498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D498 is marked for identification, and once the new version where paragraph 28 is taken out is uploaded and 1993 corrected -- I would rather not do that. That's clearly on the transcript at this moment, and I'm always a bit hesitant to make smaller changes within a document. But it's clearly on the transcript that goes without saying that 1996 is the right date. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first go to the associated exhibits, if you take them one by one, Mr. Lukic, then. The first one being?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1D... let me just have a look. On your list, I have got three associated exhibits or is it -- we have two lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two different lists, perhaps. I have one which is at the bottom dated the 2nd of May, 2014, but that's not the final one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. 1D2524, Mr. Groome. Which is SFOR Sarajevo BH, letter to the minister, Mr. Lazarevic. That's at least the description I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Lukic could indicate where in the statement the witness talks about this, and maybe address the particularities of the exhibit. When I reviewed the exhibit, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- not apparent to me how it was associated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also does not appear in annex B to the motion, the 92 ter motion, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 23. So -- it says: "My appointment to this duty is reflected in document 65 ter 1D2524, which also shows that my appointment was approved by SFOR."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we look at the exhibit itself, there appears to be, I think, four documents. The first one appears to be correspondence related to the assignment of Nikola Delic, the second one purports to be from SFOR and includes a reference to the witness as well as other VRS officers and their assignments. The letter appears to be a response to a letter from Minister Lazarevic dated the 12th of March 2001, but I note and draw the Chamber's attention the letter also seems to bear a fax stamp from either the 12th of May 2000 or 5th of December 2000 depending on whether the fax machine was set to the American standard or the European standard, and it does appear to be from a US general. The third document contains blanks and is purporting to be signed by Manojlo Milovanovic. Again, it isn't clear what the relevance of the document is. And finally there is a decree announcing the retirement of General Milovanovic. And again, I query how this is relevant or associated to the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I take it that you want to sort out this or?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can sort this out, but we included that document as we found it uploaded. I was not sure whether I should break down that documents uploaded by the Prosecution, and I take only one page from those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that you sit together with Mr. Groome during the break, try to find out how and what is the relevance, that you then isolate that from other irrelevant materials, and that you come back to us to see whether part of the document for which we find the ERN number in paragraph 23, whether that still is to be tendered or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may also assist Mr. Lukic and the Chamber to note that the Prosecution does not challenge any of the assignments that General Lalovic had during his career, so I'm not sure that any of it would be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: His approval by SFOR, I don't know what the relevance of that is and I don't know whether SFOR, what kind of an approval that is. But, of course, we do not look into the documents unless they come to us and once they are tendered. Mr. Lukic, please reconsider in the absence of any challenge to the appointments, and if you still think you need some, please sit together with Mr. Groome and see what you can leave out and what still remains relevant in this respect. Yes. That was about 1D2524. Next one, Mr. Groome -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next one was uploaded. Also it was a huge document. Actually, not huge, but probably almost 100 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Large.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now we have this number with A which actually deals only with one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That 1D2525a. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's actually two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Command of the 1st -- combat report extract of 1D2025.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And reference is in paragraph 29 of the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, when I read the document I did not see any reference to any location that was directly relevant to these proceedings so I -- again I question the relevance of this document, although I do accept that it -- it is mentioned by the witness in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to paragraph 29 in the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the document is signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Document is signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That does not necessarily make it relevant, but -- and we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I note that the copy that's uploaded in e-court does not appear to have the signature of the witness that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's typed. Typewritten name. I'm sorry, my mistake. Because it's a cable document, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see there's an information report sent in relation to this on the 1st of June. But that is not about ... no, that's about 28. Relevance, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apart from being signed by the witnesses. I mean, not everything that is signed by a witness makes it relevant for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document further elaborates the claim from the paragraph 29. And we -- here we have that the witness in this paragraph claims that Muslim forces were much better equipped than the VRS and that they were taking the initiative in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from this document, it is obvious that actually at that time offensives were launched and attacks and obvious that initiative in 1994 was on Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I don't see the direct relevance but I'll defer to the Chamber. If the Chamber thinks that it can be assists by the document, then I certainly have no strong objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I understand the hesitation by the Prosecution as it not being part of their case, that one party was stronger or that in combat one party took an initiative or not, that that's not central in their case. Is that well understood, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's even more specific than that, Your Honour. The locations referred to in this engagement, the only marginal relevance is that a road between Sarajevo and Srbinje was -- there was an effort to cut it off. But as far as I can tell, nothing else seems to be directly relevant to the matters being discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very important X and Muslim forces were actually launching offensives from Sarajevo to go through these areas and to connect with Gorazde and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be admitted. Madam Registrar, 1D02525a will receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D499 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D499 is admitted into evidence. Any -- that's all, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all. Then if you have any further questions for the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just read very short statement summary. As a professional soldier, General Lalovic served in Zagreb, Croatia, for 15 years. He left Croatia in 1991 and relocated to Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the eve of the armed conflict, Mr. Lalovic was situated in Sarajevo, and he witnessed the events that took place in the city in spring of 1992. He will testify about the blockades of roads and the JNA facilities and barracks. He will describe the attacks on the JNA vehicles and personnel. Mr. Lalovic will speak about the personnel of Muslim ethnicity leaving the ranks of the JNA. The witness will testify about his encounters with General Ratko Mladic. And General Lalovic will also describe his post-war professional engagement. And that was a short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions, you may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have just a few questions for General Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, once again, General. Let me ask you: Do you know when roadblocks, the barricades started to be set up in Sarajevo and who did it first?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: The first barricades in Sarajevo were set up on the 1st of March, 1992, by Muslims. The purpose was to limit movement in the city of Sarajevo and to create disruption. The barricades were manned by armed civilians who stopped cars and passers-by sought to see their documents. Sometimes they took away IDs from individuals and prohibited further movement. Considering that chaos began to reign, the discussion was made to form joint patrols from members of the 605th Motorised Regiment, of which I was a member, and members of the special unit of the republic SUP, secretariat for internal affairs of Bosnia Herzegovina. The commander of that unit was Dragan Dikic and one of his assistants was Zoran Cegar. These patrols were set up and they acted jointly in the territory of the city of Sarajevo and around it. They disarmed the armed civilians on barricades. They prevented certain features, especially military installations, from being surrounded and blocked and enabled movement in the city of Sarajevo and around it. That lasted until the month of April. When interethnic relations became more difficult, then tensions were heightened in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any killings in Sarajevo against JNA members in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I've already said that the first mortar attack against the Command of the 2nd Military District was on the 22nd April 1992. I can't remember the exact date now, but three days after that attack, close to the Military District Command, two unarmed soldiers from the command of the garrison were killed in a cafe. Those soldiers had stopped at that cafe to have a drink because it was close, and that's where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you witness any propaganda against the JNA; and which media spread that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: As interethnic tensions became worse and the sentiment against the JNA became negative, psychological propaganda increased, and negative information was increasingly spread against the JNA. The culmination was on the 22nd April 1992 with that mortar attack against the Military District Command and the attack on a column of soldiers in Dobrovoljacka Street. At the moment of that mortar attack, Radio Television Sarajevo, who was at the forefront of these activities, stopped the regular broadcast and informed citizenry that the Yugoslav People's Army had opened artillery fire against the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina which, of course, wasn't true. The same happened on the 3rd of May when a column of JNA troops were attacked in Dobrovoljacka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During those days was there an infantry attack against the Command of the 2nd Military District, were the guards attacked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember the exact date in April, but a civilian motor vehicle was passing by the command, and somebody in that car opened fire at the guard standing outside the command. The guard was wounded, and the rest of the guards opened fire at the vehicle, on which occasion three persons were killed. When the on-site investigation was conducted, it was found that the passengers in that car were in civilian clothes. They were armed, they had a combat set of ammunition, and even explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have paragraphs -- first the statement of Mr. Lalovic, D498, MFI'd. And we need paragraphs 13, 14, and 15 on the screen. I don't know about your screens, but I have nothing on mine. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now have something on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English version, we can see all three paragraphs. In B/C/S, that's enough. You don't have to move to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in these paragraphs, you describe the attack against the JNA hall in Sarajevo. Could you tell us if any members of the JNA tried to lift the blockade off Colonel Suput and his group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: When Colonel Suput with his group was ambushed and fire was opened on them, and when they organised a defence and couldn't move further towards the JNA hall, which they wanted to unblock, the commander of the sabotage detachment, Captain First Class Marko Labudovic who was at the military hospital in Sarajevo with part of his detachment, set out to help Colonel Suput, unblock him, and then continue jointly to lift the blockade of the JNA hall. Captain Labudovic set out with two Pinzgauers with 20 men in them. When they got to Skenderija, they were ambushed from all sides and strong infantry fire was opened on them, and they suffered huge losses. Four officers were killed; seven soldiers were killed; and six were wounded. Only three soldiers managed to get away by the skin of their teeth with the help of a passer-by, and they were not hurt. The Muslim forces used street-car wires to burn the bodies of the dead and even the wounded soldiers. Captain Marko Labudovic was lying there until the evening seriously wounded and bleeding and dying. The Muslim forces did not allow anyone to approach him and assist him. Towards the evening, the Muslims were passing by in their vehicles and drove over Captain Labudovic's dead body, and that was shown on television. Four officers were killed there: Captain First Class Marko Labudovic, Lieutenant Obrad Gvozdenovic, Lieutenant Ivan Cvetkovic, and Lieutenant Nihad Kastrati.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nihad Kastrati is which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Albanian. And he remained in the unit until the end, until he got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber misses the exact relevance of this. The witness describes which outright could be considered as awful behaviour by -- apparently by the Muslims. But the relevance for this case -- and I do not know to what extent it is contested by the Prosecution that Muslim forces or paramilitary forces or sometimes, perhaps, even civilians may have behaved in a totally unacceptable way but that doesn't make it directly relevant for the case. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Without commenting on whether or not I agree with what General Lalovic has just given evidence about, it's certainly our position that this is not relevant to the case. General Mladic is not charged with starting the war, just simply his conduct during it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we have testimony of Expert Witness Donja who testified on Sarajevo, and his complete testimony is -- is in direct contradiction with this testimony of General Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that we'll have to review then exactly the -- to what extent it clearly contradicts whether Donja's report excludes these events to have happened or similar events to have happened. But please proceed at this moment. I just want to let you know that for the core of the case against Mr. Mladic -- Mr. Mladic, who is by the way is invited to remain seated. Mr. Mladic, you know you should be seated. You can consult with counsel even in a seated passion. And we are close to a break anyhow and then you'll have ample opportunity to consult. But please proceed, meanwhile, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can -- at this moment, if there is any urgent matter, you can speak with Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Mladic, and in five minutes you have ample opportunity to further consult with Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of those two days, the 2nd and 3rd May, 1992, how many members of the army were killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd and 3rd May 1992 from the 65th Motorised Regiment, 14 soldiers and officers were killed and ten members were wounded. In total in the command of the 2nd Military District, 42 persons were killed and over 20 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing briefly. Do you know anything about the attack in Dobrovoljacka Street? That's my last question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd and 3rd May, I happened to be in Lukavica in the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks. Part of the column that had been attacked arrived at those barracks; officer, soldiers, and civilians in vehicles, and I saw them with my own eyes. When they arrived and got out of the vehicles, they were half naked, barefoot, sometimes only in underwear, disarmed. They were crying, falling to the ground, knocked their heads against walls and trees, in shock from the mistreatment and the shooting that had happened in the Dobrovoljacka Street and which they survived. Those people were saying that the Muslim paramilitaries took them out of the vehicles, lined them up, disarmed them, made them undress, made them strip, took away their personal belongings, anything they had on them, and then ordered them to lie down on the metalled road. And then one of the Muslims would show up and open volleys of automatic fire at them. Some were killed. Some were wounded. Some, the lucky ones, survived. That's how Colonel Bosko Mihajlovic, Colonel Mira Sokic, were killed. Colonel Ratko Katalina [phoen] was wounded, as well as Colonel Josip Ivanovic. I know that in that column Colonel Radulovic, head of the medical service of the 2nd Military District, was killed. He was in an ambulance, a marked ambulance, and when he opened the door to speak to those people who were doing that, people in civilian clothes but armed, he opened the door of the vehicle and told them, People, what are you doing? And one of the members of the Muslim forces opened fire and killed him on the spot without a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's all we had in direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We'll take the break first, Mr. Groome. Again, the time indicated for cross-examination was two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. And we will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start the cross-examination of the witness, yes, Mr. Ivetic is here. I think the last -- I would say extensive submission the Chamber received is that of the 26th of May, 2014. Mr. Ivetic, since I did not know exactly whether the Prosecution wants to add anything, I at least gave an opportunity to the Defence to further express itself. There's no need to repeat that because that's -- well, I wouldn't say a lengthy filing but at least it's eight pages. If we leave out the first and the last one, it's still six pages of substantial comment dealing with Aleksovski, et cetera. Is there anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, except to point out in addition to that filing that Your Honours mentioned, we also made significant reference to the same issue in one confidential reply of 5 May 2014 and one public reply of 15 May 2014 in relation to Rule 92 ter submissions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- to the extent we have not looked at that yet, and I must admit that my recollection doesn't serve me immediately, but I think, as a matter of fact, in discussing and preparing a decision that we paid attention to that but we'll verify it and we'll then give our decision preferably still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be allowed just to make one observation. We're now I believe six or seven witnesses into the Defence case and there have been occasions where, I think, that if this procedure had been followed that the cross-examination would have been shorter, so I think having coming this far I do think there will be some tangible benefits to be achieved if the Chamber were inclined to grant this relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can, and there my recollection serves me well, that the element of timing certainly is being considered by the Chamber at this moment, whether it saves time or not. If there's nothing else, Mr. Ivetic, don't feel obliged to stay with us, although it is always a pleasure to you have in court. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, General Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it would be fairer to you and more efficient in my examination of you if you had a copy of your statement in hard copy before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So unless there's an objection from the Defence and the Chamber permits, I'd ask that the witness be a handed a clean copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Currently I am a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in addition to receiving a pension, do you engage in any paid work at the moment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I do. Twenty days ago I began working for a company near the town of Brus in Serbia in the village of Plese. There's a refrigeration plant for fruit processing there, and I am now managing that plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now just make sure that I understand in general terms your statement, and that's one of the reasons why I've provided with you a hard copy. The first eight paragraphs of your statement relate to your military career; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And paragraphs 9 to 17 concern events leading up to the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraphs 18 and 19, they return to your military career; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we see at paragraphs 20 and 21, you deal with interaction that you personally had with General Mladic while he was chief of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then at paragraphs 22 to 25, we return to a discussion of your career; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 26 to 27, you deal with matters related to General Mladic while he was a fugitive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic at the time I discussed in these paragraphs was not a fugitive, as far as I know. I don't know what your interpretation is though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in a few moments. But it certainly is about your interaction with General Mladic or matters related to him after the conflict was over. In order for the transcript to record your answer, you have to actually say something.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, as you put it. In this part the paragraphs 25 and 26 and what I said therein pertains to my contacts with General Mladic after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I did say, though, that General Mladic was not a fugitive at the time, although you used that term. I was not aware of him being a fugitive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'll talk about that in a few minutes but I do simply want to make sure I understand the general import of your statement. Now, paragraph 28 has been now struck from your -- your evidence. And finally, paragraph 29 relates to document D499 in evidence, and you -- would you agree with me that deals primarily with matters related to the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let's go back now to the two paragraphs where you give evidence about General Mladic during the conflict. I want to first draw your attention to paragraph 20. Now, the main point of paragraph 20, as I read it, is that General Mladic was aware of the international laws applicable during the war and that he emphasised that you and others should act in accordance with them. Is that a correct summary of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your view was General Mladic fully versed in the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty that he was fully versed. But having taken the courses he had, taking into account his rank, and the position he was at, I would be inclined to believe that he was pretty familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you be inclined to believe that he was pretty familiar with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you be inclined to believe that he was familiar with the prohibitions against genocide?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about the prohibitions against crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was. You've asked me that already and I answered. I can't say to what extent and it wasn't up to me to check, but this is merely a belief of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 21 states that you had the opportunity or an opportunity to see Mladic in Kalinovik during Lukavac 93 operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so that we are clear, was this in a professional context or in a social context?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: We met for the first time in Trnovo when it was liberated. It was a professional encounter. Later, we met several other times in that professional capacity, given the fact that at the time we did not have time to socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you gave your statement to the Defence, you intended to provide all of the evidence that you believe was relevant to the Chamber's consideration of this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there any information now that you're here that you think now is relevant but you'd like an opportunity to provide that evidence to the Chamber, or have you provided all of your relevant evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I have no other information. I think I said all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the conflict you were in the Herzegovina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brigade carried out combat operations in the area of the Herzegovina Corps on its right flank, where the Herzegovina and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps met.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, do you accept that you did not witness - that is, personally see or hear events - directly related to the crimes charged in the indictment against General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any details of the indictment, but to my knowledge in terms of how familiar I am with that indictment, I can say that I was not directly involved in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Lalovic, let's go back to paragraph 21, and you state that you had an opportunity to see General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- first of all, I think the witness rightly commented to your question that he may not be familiar with all the details of the indictment, and, Mr. Groome, I think that appropriately would have to have been asked to him first. And, second, I think your question was about knowledge of event, whereas, the answer of the witness was about involvement in events, which is not the same. So if you'd please seek to clarify that, not necessarily in one or two questions but keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me take His Honour's counsel and ask you more particular questions: Are you aware that the indictment charges General Mladic with crimes related to Srebrenica in 1995. Have you heard my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I have. I am aware that he was charged with that, but that's all all I now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You weren't present in Srebrenica in July 1995, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He is also charged with crimes arising out of the siege of Sarajevo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the period of the conflict, were you at the time assigned to duty in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then, finally, he is charged with some crimes that occurred in the municipalities in 1992 through 1995, mostly under -- in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. Were you ever assigned to duty in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about events that transpired in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we can now turn to paragraph 21, where you say had you an opportunity to see General Mladic. My first question is, and -- I'm sorry, that you saw him during Lukavac 93. Did you see him in the forward command post in Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was a forward command post of the Herzegovina Corps. The corps command commanded its units from that position, taking part in the Lukavac 93 operation. General Lukavac came there to meet with General Grubac, where General Grubac briefed him on the situation. That is when I had the occasion to encounter General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to read you how the English record has recorded your answer and ask you whether it's correct. You have been recorded as saying General Lukavac came there to meet with General Grubac. Did you intend that to be your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: General who?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way: Who was the general that came to meet General Grubac? Was it General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was General Mladic, commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: He came to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Operation Lukavac 93 was a remember complex operation but it is one that the Chamber should have the benefit of your evidence about. What I'm going to do is read you three short paragraphs summarising the operation, and I'll ask you whether you agree with what I've said. At the end of reading that summary of the operation, I'll give you an opportunity to add any additional information you wish. Can we agree to proceed in that fashion? Again, I need you to answer for it to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. "Operation Lukavac 93 lasted between the beginning of July 1993 to mid-August 1993. The primary objectives of this operation were: One, to directly link the Herzegovina region to the rest of Republika Srpska; and two, to sever the Muslim supply route to Gorazde. The VRS began its offensive on the 2nd to 3rd of July when Tactical Group Kalinovik attacked towards the Rogoj pass from the south," and that's R-o-g-o-j. "VRS forces broke through ABiH defences to seize the Rogoj pass and the town of Trnovo eight days later." Do you agree with my summary of the operation so far?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, I agree. However, the forces of the VRS did not occupy or take Trnovo but liberated it. Before the war, Trnovo had been more a Serb than a Muslim town. That is why I say that they liberated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let me continue. "After seizing Trnovo, VRS troops then advanced west towards Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica. VRS forces also advanced to the centre of the Bosnian government's Gorazde supply route and thus linked the Herzegovina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was pushed east into Gorazde enclave and the VRS succeeded in destroying the supply corridor to Gorazde. The VRS then tried to destroy the supply line into Sarajevo over Mounts Igman and Bjelasnica." Do you agree with my summary of that portion of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with that as well. Although, I don't know whether there may have been an interpretation mistake when I heard that it was the goal of the VRS to destroy the supply line from Igman to Sarajevo. The VRS had -- had as its objective to cut off that supply line rather than destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: If I may. These objectives were set by a superior command. I am aware of them, but there was no need for me to know them necessarily. I don't know what is the importance of me agreeing or disagreeing. If my superior command during the war set an objective and issued a task to me, it was my obligation to see it through and to achieve the objective set. However, you have been referring to some superior command objectives which I needn't necessarily know as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I want to read the last portion of the operation and once again ask you to comment on whether you agree with my recounting of it. "On the 31st of July, the VRS launched a surprise attack on the summit of Mount Bjelasnica. VRS troops advanced about 10 kilometres up Bjelasnica and Igman over the next four days. This succeeded in cutting the last Bosnian government supply line into Sarajevo. The VRS held these positions until it withdrew under pressure from the international community and threats of action by NATO. The VRS withdrew from Mount Igman by the 19th of August, 1993." Do you agree with that portion of my summary of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Please read out the first part again concerning the 31st of July. What happened then? I didn't pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read that first sentence: "On 31 July, the VRS launched a surprise attack on the summit of Mount Bjelasnica."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it could have been on the 31st of July to attack Bjelasnica if there was combat along that axis as of the 2nd of July. When the attack on Rogoj began on the 2nd of July, that is when operations began and Trnovo and Rogoj were liberated. Our forces went further afield to Bjelasnica. In my understanding, it couldn't have been a surprise attack on Bjelasnica. I would call it something that would have been expected. You asked me whether I agree and I'm trying to answer in a profession way. To me, professionally speaking, it could have not been a surprise attack on Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was something to be expected. I have no knowledge about the latter part of what you read out. As to whether the supply line to Sarajevo was completely cut and when the forces were pulled from Igman and why. I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, what is your best recollection as to when the VRS launched an attack on the summit of Mount Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You said when it was. I don't know when exactly it was. I don't recall the date. I just told that you it was no surprise attack. It was to be expected. As a soldier to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, there's no --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: -- there's a great it difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- need to repeat your answer. You've already told us that you don't believe it was a surprise particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 30647 on our screens. It is an order for further operations dated 26 June 1993 and bears the title: "Lukavac 93."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It will be up on your screen in a minute. While we're waiting for that, General, can I ask you to confirm that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps also had an opportunity role to play in Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It certainly did, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can now see the document on the screen. I'm going to give you a moment to familiarise yourself with the details of the document. Then I'm going to read from this first page which sets out the current assessment of the situation. It states: "By fighting our forces and the HVO, the Muslim leadership is trying to maintain its domination over Central Bosnia, solve the issue of Vares, and then through a great offensive, to unblock Sarajevo, establish wider corridor between Sarajevo and Gorazde and connect Gorazde with Zepa and Srebrenica." My question to you is very simply: Does this agree with your recollection of the situation that prevailed at the end of June in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment upon this. It is an order issued by the SRK which was never sent to me. I really cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you are putting this question to me when I was not a member of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me intervene for a moment. Witness, the question was whether what you now read or what is read to you, whether that is in line with the situation you remember that it existed at the end of June 1993. So you're not asked to say, I saw the document, or -- just what is read to you: The situation described in that document, is that consistent with your recollection of the situation at the end of June 1993? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in June 1993 was as follows. Trnovo was in Muslim hands, and the communication between Foca-Trnovo-Sarajevo was cut off, or Kalinovik-Trnovo-Sarajevo, the roads. Then the Muslim forces had established a corridor from Konjic via Trnovo to Gorazde, and they supplied their forces in Gorazde through that corridor. That was the situation. Now, if this coincides with that, that is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It seems that, at least in part, this comports with your recollection. Could I ask now -- well, let me ask you this: Do you recall that one of the primary objectives of this operation that you personally participated in was to link the Herzegovina Corps and the Sarajevo Corps so that there would be no enemy forces between the two corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That was one of the objectives. It was. And the forces of the Herzegovina Corps and the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps took part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it also an important objective of this operation to prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know in which sense. Who would prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo? I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the operation was, in part, to create conditions for the take-over of Sarajevo, or possible take-over of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to page 3 of the English and -- I'm sorry. Page 3 in both. In the original it is very bottom of page 3 but does carry over to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you a passage with respect to the detailed objectives of the SRK. "Take possession of buildings on Igman and Bjelasnica, preventing manoeuvre of the Muslim forces to and from Sarajevo, prevent its unblocking, and create conditions for its take-over."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we advance the page for the -- in the B/C/S so that the witness can see the remainder of what I've read. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read this. It was on the other page. Could you get this one back?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll go back to page 3 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question to you is: Do you agree that I have accurately read what the objectives of the SRK were as reported in this order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: If that is what is written here, then that is probably the case. But I was not aware of these objectives in such detail because, again, I'm telling you, I did not receive this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that this document be marked for identification. I intend to use it with another witness later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30647 receives number P6549, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Lalovic you're from Kalinovik; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's the same place where General Mladic is from; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. General Mladic is from one village and I am from another village. But we're both from the municipality of Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how far away are the two villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're about 4 or 5 kilometres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you still have a home in Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. In 1971, my father moved --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: -- out of Kalinovik to Lukavica near Sarajevo and that's where he built a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Don't need all that detail but if you can simply just confine yourself to the precise question. Did you know General Mladic growing up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him when I was growing up because General Mladic, as a very young man, left Kalinovik to continue his schooling, so I did not have an opportunity to meet him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now General Mladic's grandfather's name is Filip Lalovic. Do you recognise the name Filip Lalovic, same last name as you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I know that his name was Filip Lalovic and I knew this grandfather Filip Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there a relationship, family relationship between Filip Lalovic and your Lalovic family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: In order for you to understand that, allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: The Lalovics are the most numerous family in Kalinovik. They've been living there for -- or, rather, in at least half of the villages of the municipality of Kalinovik. General Lalovic's mother and grandfather Filip lived in the village of Kuta, and my family lived in the village of Vlaholje. The distance between these two villages is also approximately 4 to 5 kilometres. The Lalovic family, since they are so spread out, they -- all members are not that close to one another anymore. So I am not a close relation of grandfather Filip and the mother of General Lalovic -- oh, sorry, General Mladic. But at any rate, we are distantly related. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure that the record has recorded your evidence correctly. I'm going to read what's been recorded now. I think there may have been a mistake. I'd just ask you to simply correct it without going into the entire answer again. The records you as saying: "General Lalovic's mother," possibly grandmother, "and grandfather Filip --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, that was the mother of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So General Mladic's mother and General Mladic's grandfather lived in the village of Kuta? And we know how far away it was from yours.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Kuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now how would you characterise your personal relationship with General Mladic at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: My personal relationship with General Mladic is one that I would describe as a professional relationship of two professionals. If we're speaking in the present, two generals. If we are talking about then, that is to say, the time of war, then a general and a lieutenant-colonel or rather colonel or rather a relationship between the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of one of the brigades of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P352 be brought to our screens. Now, General Lalovic, in paragraph 12, you recount that General Kukanjac requested Ejub Ganic to end attacks on the JNA in response to an attack on the 22nd of April, 1992, that you describe in the preceding paragraph. I've read your evidence. I'm not asking you to go through it again. I have one very simple question. My question is: How did you know what General Kukanjac knew? What's the basis of that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't find it clear. What is that I know that General Kukanjac knew, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you know that General Kukanjac made this request of Ejub Ganic to end attacks on the JNA. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that from Colonel Suput, the commander of my regiment. At the time when this attack took place, Colonel Suput was at the command of the 2nd Military District with part of the Protection Regiment that was securing the command of the 2nd Military District, whereas I was at the Butila barracks with the remainder of the regiment that had been stationed there. And Colonel Suput and I were in constant communication along several channels; radio communication, telephone. And he said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now could I ask that we go to page 277 in the original and page 268 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you an entry that is in -- is from the military notebook of General Mladic, and you are mentioned in these notebooks in several places. The entry that I want to draw your attention to is one in which it appears you and others met with General Mladic on the 9th of May, 1992. And my first question while you're looking at that first page: Am I correct that this would be three days before the VRS was established? The 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Could you please tell me what the date is exactly, when this happened, and also the place where this happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All of our knowledge is based on the notes, so now you can see it. I think we had the wrong page up there a minute ago. So my first question before we deal with the substance of this -- this entry is simply: Am I correct that the 9th of May, 1992, was three days before the VRS was established.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the entry seems to be from a meeting that General Mladic had with the 2nd Military District Command. My first question is: Is to ask you to simply confirm that this entry was made while both you and General Mladic were in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: If it was on the 9th, then, yes, we were members of the JNA; but at this meeting -- I was not at that meeting. I did not see General Mladic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if we look down, there is a reference to Colonel Milan Suput's deputy, Lieutenant-Colonel Lalovic. Do you agree that that is a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was Colonel Suput's deputy and Chief of Staff of the Protection Regiment, but I did not attend this kind of meeting on the 9th of May. I first saw General Mladic in Crna Rijeka when the Army of Republika Srpska was established and when he came to the command post. That's when I first saw him. I don't know exactly what the date was, but the army was established on the 12th of May so it must have been soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now do you recall Colonel Milan Suput going this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Suput could not been at that meeting when he was taken prisoner at the time. And he was in Muslim dungeons where he was tortured. He was taken prisoner on the 3rd of May and he was freed on the 13th of May. He was exchanged on the 13th of May at Stupska Petlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I don't believe you can be helpful interpreting some of the text in this meeting. Let me change topics. Now, General Lalovic, you are aware that several cases before this Tribunal, including this one, involved accused who are members of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You're expecting me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you would appreciate that in any case related to the members of the Main Staff the documents they received, that they authored, that they signed, that they sent to subordinates. All of these documents would be quite relevant to these trials. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All of these documents would be found in the archive of the Main Staff of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That is where they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know where the archive of the Main Staff is located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 6140 be brought to our screens. It is a statement by Manojlo Milovanovic that was given to the government of Republika Srpska. In one section of the statement, he deals with the whereabouts of this archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll give you a moment to see the first page. Then I'll ask that we go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please go to e-court page 3 in both copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in the original text, General Lalovic, could I draw your attention to the bottom of the page. In this portion of General Milovanovic's statement, he is describing his efforts to get a document from the archives of the VRS Main Staff and it recounts a conversation he had with you. "It took me until the middle of 2000 to get to the archives. Precisely on 14 June of that year, a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council was held in Crna Rijeka and I wanted to obtain some documents from the archives about the counter-attack carried out against Bihac at the end of 1994. However, Colonel Lalovic told me that the archives could not be accessed but were in a safe place." My first question is whether you acknowledge that the Lalovic that General Milovanovic is referring to is, in fact, you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Probably it is me if it says Dragan Lalovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note we can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters have difficulties in hearing you. Could you please speak into the microphone or perhaps the microphone with the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he meant me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said probably it is me if it says Dragan Lalovic. But it says Colonel Lalovic. That would still be you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's me probably. I think it's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that question be absolutely sure if we look just few sentences above where I've just read from, it says: "Mladic wished it so and then it was Colonel, and later General, Dragan Lalovic, also because Mladic wished it so." Does this eliminate any doubt that you are the Lalovic who is being referred to by General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Any doubt has been eliminated. He is talking about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were at a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council on the 14th of June, 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: The 14th of June? And what's the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 2000. According to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: A meeting of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps there's translation issue. We will check that. Do you acknowledge that you spoke with General Milovanovic with respect to his request to obtain some documents from the Main Staff archives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I do not confirm that. I don't remember him asking me that, and I would be surprised if he asked me for that. I'm surprised because General Milovanovic knows - just as I know - that, at the time, all organs of the Main Staff that went to Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: -- had their own archives with them and brought them to Bijeljina when the Main Staff was dissolved and when the General Staff headed by Pero Colic was established.
