So all organs of the Main Staff that left from Crna Rijeka to Bijeljina, they took their archives along with them. And I'm surprised, I mean, that he could have put it that way. I personally was asked by the chief of the security administration, Colonel Beara, to transport the archives of the security administration to Bijeljina and to hand it over to the new chief of the security administration, General Savcic, which is indeed what I did. If -- I don't know. I don't know. I'm surprised. I'm really surprised he could have stated something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you: When did you transfer the archives of the security administration to Bijeljina? When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That was sometime -- sometime at the end of 1996. The General Staff in Bijeljina was established in November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the -- the archive that you're referring to, was this part of the Main Staff archive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. It was part of the Main Staff archive. And Colonel Beara ordered me to take the archives to Bijeljina. All of that was packed. And they loaded this onto a vehicle and I drove that there, in boxes, and I handed that over to the new chief of the Security Administration, General Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as I understand your evidence, this portion of the Main Staff archive, you personally brought it up to Bijeljina. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, personally. I personally drove it up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you personally gave it to the new chief of Security Administration, General Savcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: General Savcic. Packed in boxes. I didn't open that when this was loaded onto the vehicle and I did not open the boxes when I brought that to him. I brought it to him and I said, Sir, Colonel Beara is sending you the archive of the Security Administration. It is in these boxes. Please appoint someone to receive this. And he asked a person to do that, and what was done with it afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just ask a couple of more questions on this topic and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll take the break in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many boxes you drove up to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in a passenger vehicle, a Golf. It could have been five or six box, maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you deny that you ever had a conversation with General Milovanovic about the location of the archives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that I ever talked to him about that. It's possible that he asked me that, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my last question for the morning is: Is there any reason that you can think of why General Milovanovic would fabricate a conversation with you about the archives of the Main Staff when giving an official statement to the Republika Srpska government?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. If you ask, Why did he do it? May call for speculation. But, Do you know of any reason? It could be any circumstance. But apart from that, the witness answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your answer is as you sit here today you know of no reason why General Milovanovic would fabricate this account of a conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that concludes that particular topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noted that Mr. Mladic, several times, expressed either agreement with or at least he sometimes spoke even a bit louder. Mr. Mladic is ordered to refrain from any expression of agreement, disagreement, appreciation, whatever, any comment on the testimony of this witness, and that should be clear to him, and I do understand from his body language that he has understood this instruction very well. We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, Mr. Groome will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Lalovic, General Milovanovic has appeared before this Chamber and therefore the Chamber will be able to make its own evaluation regarding this conversation. My simple question to you is: Do you accept that if someone did hide the Main Staff archives, evidence relevant to the Tribunal's work, that doing so would be an attempt to undermine the work of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you visit General Mladic at the Detention Unit after arriving here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you intend on visiting him before you leave The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I am permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking. You can consult with Mr. Stojanovic, if you wish, at such a level -- microphone off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing aloud. Nothing aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, making gestures does not -- is not sufficient, Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Lalovic, I don't take any issue with what you say about your military career, but do want to ask you a few questions about your time in Kosovo. Now, in your statement at paragraph 22, you say that you went to the National Defence School in Belgrade on the 1st of September, 1988. You then say: "The training was interrupted due to the breakout of war in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the bombing that commenced on 24 March 1999. Thereupon I was sent to the Pristina Corps Command where I stayed until the signing of the technical agreement of 10 June 1999." Is it your recollection that you did not go to Pristina until the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But I would like to answer the previous question you asked me. I -- I didn't answer. You asked me if I should like to visit General Mladic at the Detention Unit. Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The -- the record recorded you saying if I am permitted. Is there significant else you'd like to say in addition that you will if you are permitted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't register that my answer was, in fact, understood. It's precisely the way you say. I should like to visit him, if I am permitted. Now, if you want an answer to the second question, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right. So is it your recollection that you did not go to Pristina until 24 March 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had never been to Pristina before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the Pristina Corps was a subordinate command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this Tribunal in the judgement of Milutinovic and others, at paragraph 588 found that General Nebojsa Pavkovic decided on the 1st of February, 1999, to re-establish a forward command post for the 3rd Army in Pristina. And said: "Due to the growing complexity of the security situation in the 3rd Army's zone of responsibility during 1999, Pavkovic, by then 3rd Army commander, decided again to again establish a forward command post in Pristina on 1 February 1999." My question to you is: Might you be mistaken about when you went to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not mistaken. I went to the Pristina Corps when the bombing of the SFRY -- of the FRY - correction - had already started. The attack started on the 24th of March, 1999. That's when my training was interrupted. And not only mine, the training was interrupted in the entire National Defence school and all the schools in Belgrade and all the trainees were sent to various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I happened to be sent to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, just one correction. I think you misspoke when you first referred to September 1988 in -- on page 51, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just let me pull it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said 1988 but it should be, I suppose, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. I'm sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Could I ask that we see 65 ter 30730 on our screens. This is an order of the VJ signed by Lieutenant-General Nebojsa Pavkovic on the 2nd of February, 1999, assigning Dragan Lalovic and 16 other officers to man the forward command post in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lalovic, you can see the document on our screens. I will give you a few moments to familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, according to this order of February 1999, person by the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Lalovic was to be part of the forward command post. Is this a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's not me. At that time, I was a colonel. I was a trainee at the National Defence School and this is a lieutenant-colonel, Dragan Lalovic, who had communications, in fact, signals, as his military specialty, and I believe he was chief of communications at the Command of the 3rd Army. I know him. He is a native of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the same command post that you then say you went to on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you say you -- you say in paragraph 22 of your statement that you stayed in Pristina until the 10th of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So between the 24th of March and the 10th of June, 1999, you were present in the forward command post in Pristina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the command of the Pristina Corps in that period. In the operations and training. They defined my assignment as assisting them, which means I was not appointed to any command position. Instead, I organised training and helped the chief of that section. I did whatever was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, as I'm sure you know, a judgement was entered with respect to Mr. Pavkovic and others on the 26th of February, 2009, in which Mr. Pavkovic was sentenced to 22 years. I'm going to read you a passage from the judgement summary and then ask you a question. "The Trial Chamber therefore finds that there was a broad campaign of violence directed against the Kosovo Albanian civilian population during the course of the NATO air strikes conducted by forces under the control of the FRY and Serbian authorities, during which there were incidents of killing, sexual assault, and the intentional destruction of mosques. It was the deliberate actions of these forces during this campaign that caused the departure of at least 700.000 Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo in the short period of time between the end of March and the beginning of June 1999." Now my question you to is the following. The judgement in this case has been affirmed on appeal. Do you accept that crimes were committed in the -- in Kosovo, as described by the -- the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no foundation for this question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to explore whether or not the witness has a bias for or against the work of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He should know facts from the trial to be able to establish -- I mean, he is not legal expert. I don't know. I really don't think this is a proper question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me then limit my question to you to factual knowledge. You were present in the command in Pristina at the time that serious crimes were committed. Were you aware of the commission of crimes by VR -- by FRY and Serbian authorities, including killing, sexual assault, and the intentional destruction of mosques? Were you aware of crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of those crimes. I was at the command of the corps where decisions were made concerning combat operations, where combat operations were planned, and they were targeting exclusively armed Siptar forces. I was not aware of those acts, nor did I see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you aware while you were present that 700.000 Kosovo Albanians were forced from their homes during these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'd like to change topics. In paragraph 22, you state: "From 15 February 1997 to the 31st of August 1998, I was the commander of military police security detachment. The detachment was established and stationed at Crna Rijeka and its duty was to secure war command posts of the VRS and General Ratko Mladic." What was your understanding of General Mladic's position at this stage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that the position of General Mladic at that stage was the same as the position of any other general of his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And let's be more specific. Tell us specifically what was your understanding of his position. What was -- what were his duties during this period? Between February 1997 and August 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was not mine to think about that. General Mladic was, by virtue of the decrees and decisions of the competent authorities, given certain appointments that went with a certain status. If his status was such that he was supposed to be at a war command position in the Army of Republika Srpska, then that's how it was. What -- what other understanding was I supposed to have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you are putting questions to the witness in relation to the position of Mr. Mladic. That is at least an ambiguous question because there are several aspects of that position. One of them, and I may perhaps ask the witness, were you aware of any indictment brought against General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, as commander of the military police security detachment, you commanded the people who were directly responsible for Mr. Mladic's security; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is very simple. During the period that you were the commander responsible for his security, what was your understanding of his title?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I said that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Just give me a minute to explain. By his position and rank according to the rules that prevailed at the time, General Mladic was one of the top military officers who were entitled to security provided by military units. The decision to form that detachment was made by the competent authority in Serbia. It was not my decision to set up that detachment, nor was it my decision to appoint myself commander of that unit. The competent authorities decided to form that unit and appoint me commander, and if they decided that I should discharge that duty, then I don't see why I should have had any doubts or refused to execute this order. If I had refused, I would have opened myself to prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the second rather lengthy answer with all I'm seeking is a simple one or two words. That's what I ask you for now. Maybe the transcript is somehow missing what you are saying. What was the command or what was the duty of Mladic during February 1997 and August 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his duty was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any access to the decrees appointing General Mladic or the orders given to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: And it was not my job to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was he stationed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic was stationed, from the beginning of March 1997, in Crna Rijeka, at the command post. After that, he left for Belgrade, and he was based in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he leave for Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: In early March 1997. I think it was the beginning of March. I don't remember the date, but I believe it was in the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to say the year again? There seems to be some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you accompanied him to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He was accompanied by the men who were told to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I ask for some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you said that from beginning of March 1997, General Mladic was stationed in Crna Rijeka. Was it in this same month - March 1997 - that he moved for Belgrade? To Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question. Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On page 58, lines 22 to 23, you said: "General Mladic was stationed, from the beginning of March 1997, in Crna Rijeka, at the command post." That is what we can find in your statement as well. Then you said he went to Belgrade at the beginning of March 1997. That means in the same month; is that correct? Or is there some confusion? Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the beginning of March 1997, General Mladic, who -- was in Crna Rijeka at his war time command post. When the war began in 1997, he left for Belgrade, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you help me? Which war are you referring to which began in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about war. I'm talking about the month of March. General Mladic was at his war time command post in Crna Rijeka until the beginning of March 1997. In the beginning of March 1997, he departed for Belgrade, Serbia. Is it clear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when -- from which time on did he reside in Crna Rijeka? When was that post set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crna Rijeka was a command post of the war time staff of the VRS, was established on the 12th of May, 1992, when the VRS was established. That's where the Main Staff of the VRS was based. And when it was disbanded in November 1996, that's when the Main Staff of the VRS was disbanded, and a General Staff was set up in Bijeljina, headed by General Pero Colic. General Mladic spent all his time there and never went anywhere until he departed for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now where in Belgrade did General Mladic go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic left for Belgrade to live in his apartment, in his house. I know that soon after he arrived, the wedding of his son Darko was organised, and he attended that wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during this period, you were still responsible for his security; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the security unit, whereas the direct security detail around him consisted of men whom I designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did he remain in his apartment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember. I really can't tell you. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Until August 1998, do you know if General Mladic moved out of his apartment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. General Mladic never moved out of his apartment. It's still his apartment, and his wife still lives there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you to carefully listen to the answer [sic]. The answer was not whether he still owned that apartment and whether his family was living there, but Mr. Groome is interested in knowing on when, in fact, Mr. Mladic discontinued to live in that apartment. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I just did. I said that General Mladic never moved out of that apartment. He never stopped living there. Occasionally he left the Belgrade apartment to go to some military facilities. And, again, occasionally he returned from those facilities to the apartment. That is why I am saying that he never left the apartment. I don't know what you understand by that term. In my understanding, if someone leaves or moves out of an apartment, they leave it for good. I don't know what your meaning of it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My meaning is that you spend most of your time not in that apartment any further. That is what I understand by to discontinue living there. Doesn't mean that you never go back but it means that you are most of the days not living in that apartment and that have you other places where you spend most of your days and nights. That's what I understand by living or not living in an apartment. Could you tell us from when on Mr. Mladic did not any further spend most of his days and nights in his apartment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I commanded the unit, which was between the 15th of February, 1997 and the 24th of February, 2001. General Mladic occasionally stayed had his Belgrade apartment and sometimes went to certain military facilities where he spent certain periods of time. I can't tell you exactly how much time he spent in his apartment as opposed to the time spent in those facilities. The last time I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking that. I asked when most of the time he did not further stay in his apartment. I give you one last chance to answer that question. If not, I just have to establish that you are not directly responding to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to provide a direct answer, but I can't because General Mladic spent some time in February, the last time in February 2001 where I saw him for the last time, just before I left my position for a more senior one in the 7th Corps of the VRS where I was appointed the Chief of Staff. That is why I can't answer your question directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was then -- in February 2001, was Mr. Mladic spending most of his time habitually living in his apartment in Belgrade? Would he be there four, five, six days a week, or would he be there once every month, or perhaps once every second month, or? And I'm now talking about the time when you said you -- February 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was then staying most of the time in his apartment in Belgrade, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, at that time, he was mostly in his apartment. At least to the extent I am able to recollect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, so I understand your evidence correctly, you were responsible for General Mladic's security between February 1997 and February 2001, a period of four years; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you said just a moment ago in a response to a question by Judge Orie that he sometimes went to certain military facilities where he spent certain periods of time. Can you please name those military facilities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I can. Just before that, let me tell you this: Out of the four years, I spent one year at the National Defence School between the 1st of September, 1998, and the 1st of September, 1999. That -- during that time, I was not at that position. I apologise, could you now repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps next time you first answer the question and only then tell us what you apparently find important to tell us. The question simply was to name those military facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I held the position of the unit commander, General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, [Indiscernible]. No. Name of the military facilities where Mr. Mladic spent yet undefined times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic spent some time in the military facility at Rajac as well as the Stragari military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he also stay at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- and at any time you were not there, did he then spend time in the facility just mentioned by Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. While I was there, in barracks, while I was at that position, there was personnel in the Topcider barracks, meaning the personnel engaged in providing security for General Mladic. So he may have come to talk to them on occasion, but I don't know whether he did. I wasn't posted there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, you're saying that personnel engaged in providing security for Mladic, these are personnel under your command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: They were under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for what period of time were they at Topcider -- was your personnel at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say precisely. I know that they were there when the air campaign started. They were there then on the 24th of March. I don't know how much earlier they were sent there. I can't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that his presence at these military facilities was not public information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying information that he was at these facilities, including Topcider, was something that was considered to be secret?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was considered secret for many; although, for some, it wasn't. It was secret for most. Usually you don't publicise where a particular person that a security escort is being provided for is at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it something that was kept secret from other military personnel at these facilities, including Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that during the times he was at these military facility, including Topcider, it was known by other military personnel stationed there, that General Mladic was staying there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. [In English] This gentleman never confirmed that Mr. Mladic was in Topcider and it was proposed to him now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He also did not exclude for that possibility. So I think if the question would have been phrased correctly by Mr. Groome, it would have been military facilities potentially including Topcider. That would be the right phrasing of the question. But the witness didn't exclude for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When he was enumerating the objects, he knew he was enumerating and he gave us two names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then the position was, I mean by the Prosecution, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then he answered the question by saying that his people who were -- to give security to Mr. Mladic were at Topcider and that he would not exclude for the possibility that Mr. Mladic went there to see him. That's exactly the -- what I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he -- but to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers]... be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have -- well, if you go somewhere then you are there, Mr. Lukic. Perhaps not permanently. But let's stay out of that at this moment. Let's return to the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you repeat the question, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, in light of Mr. Lukic's comments if the people under your command assigned to take care of General Mladic are somewhere, is it your expectation as a commander that they're with him, the people that are protecting him are there with the person they're assigned to protect? Is that not a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It is not a logical conclusion to be drawn. First of all, I didn't say that General Mladic stayed at the Topcider barracks. I said that I do not exclude the possibility that he came to see them. If he did, to talk to them, it was perhaps for half an hour or an hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, how -- could you tell us, because you're now repeating what you said already and what I summarised and I didn't hear from Mr. Lukic that I wasn't summarising it accurately, you said he would be there for half an hour or an hour. You couldn't exclude for that. How do you know that? Why couldn't he have been there for three or four hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because I received reports from the people who were there, the people who provided security detail for General Mladic. They were billeted in one building of the Topcider barracks, while General Mladic was either in his apartment or in the military facility. From there, the personnel went to wherever General Mladic went if he was in movement. They provide security at his -- the place of his apartment and in the facility as well. So from the Topcider barracks, people were dispatched to go about their security tasks. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, of course, Mr. Groome draws your attention to that it seems not to be very practical to billet those who are providing security for Mr. Mladic at a place and specifically a place where he never was or only exceptionally for half an hour or an hour. That is what Mr. Groome is drawing your attention to. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can comment. I'm a professional in that regard. I was a member of the military police for 15 years, and I was engaged in such affairs. When a person is being secured, that person is never staying with the people providing security. He's always in one place and the personnel in another. They are never together and this case was such. We provided security for General Mladic in his apartment. We can't stay there. I needed to have accommodation for the people, a place where they can shower, eat, and function normally in order to be rested and ready for the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. I can understand that if we're talking about an apartment where an individual is living. I have more difficulties in understanding this if someone is residing in a military facility where there may be, like in Topcider, may be facilities security as well in the same premises or nearby, to take their showers and to sleep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he went to Rajac, he was accompanied by a group of people who were billeted in that facility. General Mladic would stay in one building and the people in another. When he went to Stragari, that facility already had its own security provided by the Army of Yugoslavia and then General Mladic was accompanied by a very small group, like two escorts and a driver at the most. They would then be accommodated in one of the buildings in the facility where General Mladic was, close to him. However, the facility at Topcider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was something we considered to a base for the unit which provided security for him. They spent their time there. When needed, they left the base to perform their tasks wherever it was that General Mladic went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. Do I understand that you were fully familiar with all the details of the whereabouts of General Mladic during that period of time? If even occasional visits of half an hour or one hour to Topcider were reported to you, if your people had to accompany him when he was in his apartment, when you were aware of all the facilities where your people went and stayed when General Mladic was there? Do I understand that you had full oversight of every movement of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One couldn't say so. I did not have full oversight. I wasn't there permanently. Most of my time was spent at Crna Rijeka, but I did receive reports from my subordinates. So I can say that in 90 per cent of the cases, I knew where General Mladic was, or I learned of it later. Sometimes they wouldn't notify me immediately where he was to go. There was no logic that they should share that via communication links. They were sufficiently independent and could organise themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, this -- where we're -- you're at now is 90 per cent of the time between February 1997 and February 2001, you knew where General Mladic was? Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You understood it well. But I can't reconstruct everything. If you were to ask me to what date to what date he was in his apartment or at Stragari or at Rajac, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the 11th July 1996 three Judges of this Tribunal issued an international arrest warrant for General Mladic. Earlier today, you said that you were aware of that arrest warrant. My question to you is: Were you aware of that arrest warrant prior to taking up command in February 1997 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you point us as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where the witness said that he was aware of the arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was a response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question was put to him about awareness of an indictment and not about an arrest warrant, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The same day that the indictment was confirmed by three Judges of this Tribunal on the 11th of July 1996, they issued an international arrest warrant. Were you aware that there was an international arrest warrants issued by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was aware of the warrant. I learned about it from the media. As for any arrests, I don't recall that. If it was made public in the media -- well, I considered it to be one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question then is: Were you aware at the time you took command of the unit responsible for General Mladic's security, were you aware that an arrest warrant and an indictment had been issued?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I learned of it through the media. I knew that an indictment was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you aware that there has -- a sizeable monetary reward had been posted for information that could lead to his apprehension? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I could see that from the media. I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So at the time you took responsibility for his security, were you aware that there was an arrest warrant, plus a sizeable reward, for information leading to his capture. Were you aware of that at the time that you assumed command of the unit responsible for his security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that the indictment was issued, and I knew about the monetary reward. I learned it from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is: When did you learn it? Did you learn it before you assumed command in February 1997?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I learned of it around that time. I don't know whether it was before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 26 of your statement it says, in part: "At that time we provided security for General Mladic against criminals and individuals who would attempt to cause him harm in any manner." Would you have considered an effort by SFOR to apprehend General Mladic pursuant to a warrant issued by this Court to be something you would have protected General Mladic from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Any SFOR attempt would be in keeping with the arrest warrant, but it never materialised. If it had, I would have been forced to implement my task, which was to protect General Mladic at the time. At the time, there was no arrest warrant for General Mladic in my country issued by our authorities. If there was no arrest warrant, how could I allow that General Mladic be -- would be arrested if I were tasked with providing security for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I conclude from that, that you do not or did not recognise the legal authority of an arrest warrant issued by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you can conclude that. Until the International Tribunal turns to me directly or to one of my superiors requesting that we arrest him and deliver him, the question remains purely hypothetical. If it happened, then someone more senior to me, starting with the president of Republika Srpska down, would have to decide that I should deliver him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've given evidence that he travelled to Belgrade in 1997. What order or what instruction did you give the men under your command if they were to be stopped by SFOR attempting to arrest General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: When he went to Serbia, there was no possibility for him to be arrested by SFOR, and there was no need for me to issue any instructions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did he get from Crna Rijeka to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: From Crna Rijeka to Serbia, he travelled along the road from Crna Rijeka-Han Pijesak-Vlasenica and Zvornik used by all other motor vehicles. He crossed the bridge at Karakaj where the border crossing to Serbia is, just as any other person would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So again I return to my -- to my question: What did you instruct your subordinates who were responsible for his security to do if SFOR made an attempt to arrest General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even consider that variant. At the time, I had no intelligence of SFOR wanting to arrest General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that despite an arrest warrant and a reward, you never considered the possibility that SFOR would want to arrest General Mladic? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't consider that. I didn't consider the possibility because I had no such information. I have to say that sometime in mid-1996 in Vlasenica, I met with a -- an American brigade commander. I think his name was Colonel Battista [phoen]. The topic of the meeting was not General Mladic. It was something unrelated to it, concerning some soldiers who were carrying arms where they shouldn't have. And they belonged to a certain unit in Vlasenica. Then Battista said, We are not looking for General Mladic or Karadzic. He started discussing it and mentioned it along the way. He said, We're not looking for them, but if they showed up here at this moment, I would have to arrest them. That is why I didn't even consider that possibility. Secondly, no one even announced that possibility. We were in contact with SFOR and they never announced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to a break. I have one or two questions for you. You said in one of your previous answers: "Until the International Tribunal turns to me directly or to one of my superiors requesting that we arrest him and deliver him, the question remains purely hypothetical." Do I understand that you had no knowledge of the International Tribunal turning to your superiors - that means your government - to have Mr. Mladic be arrested and delivered to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, General Mladic became a wanted man in Republika Srpska in May 2000 roughly at the same time in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I don't know whether the International Tribunal or any other international institution addressed the organs of government of Republika Srpska, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the military organs directly to have General Mladic extradited. I really don't know. That did not reach me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- you learned everything from the media but not that he was wanted and to be transferred to The Hague? You thought that it was just not serious to indict him and?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't think it was not serious. I just didn't consider this indictment. I didn't. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But an indictment without an accused to appear before a court, that -- you were not aware that he -- this Tribunal really had taken every steps to secure his presence here in The Hague, including his transfer? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question by Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us you received the duty to provide security for Mr. Mladic. Who was it who gave this task to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Commander of Army of Republika Srpska, the president of Republika Srpska, who ordered the establishment of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He, that means Mr. Karadzic personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time it was Mrs. Biljana Plavsic who was the president, not Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And she ordered you to provide this security; is that correct? Personally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally. She ordered the establishment of this unit, and such orders are written up on the establishment of a unit. And then that went through the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. No one gave me a personal order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But a written order, to be the head of this unit where -- that had to provide security; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right. Written order appointing me commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you remember when this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't remember exactly when it was issued. Probably during those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, but could the witness first be escorted out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Defence told us that the witness would have to leave, I'm a bit concerned about the time. Mr. Groome, could you give us any indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think we should be able to finish today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means how much time left for Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know how much time Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if you are confident that we finish today -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I should say that I have used an hour and 15 minutes. I don't think I will use the full time that I anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me take a look, Your Honour, and I'll give a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could either communicate with Mr. Lukic and see how you divide the time. I don't know how much time Mr. Lukic would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Lukic said to me earlier today that he is available for early tomorrow morning as long as we get him out of here, so I'm not sure that time is as much a pressure as the Chamber believes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. But we follow the suggestions by the -- we'll hear from the parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think he has to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from the parties how we proceed until quarter past 2.00, and if there's any dispute in a solution, then, of course, the Chamber will take the necessary decisions. We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, meanwhile, perhaps a brief question. The focus was on arrest warrants issued 2000. I didn't hear any question about arrest warrant issued in 1995, 1996. That's -- that surprises me a bit because it was so much earlier, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour, but after the Rule 61 hearing the Chamber issued an international arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And clearly there's a fine line between the two, but it seemed to me that the more unequivocal arrest warrant was the one issued in July 1st 1996. Otherwise, I guess one would question the purpose of the Rule 61 hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's -- have the parties agreed on timing? Yes, that's appreciated. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just let me say what the agreement is. Mr. Lukic has said that has no questions. And I have -- I have 50 minutes left, I will endeavour to do it in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see how confident the Chamber is that if you reach an agreement that, without even knowing the details, that we rely that it goes well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukic has asked me to correct something with you. He says that he believes the record has incorrectly recorded what you said about when you believed General Mladic became a wanted man in Republika Srpska. So can you repeat the time-period or date when you believe he became a wanted man in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say what the exact date would be. As far as I can remember you've already asked me that and I said it was around February. Now, was it before the establishment of this unit or after that? I don't know exactly. And I think that is what I said when you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No -- okay. We'll leave it there. Mr. Lukic can clarify more if he needs to. Now, you've said that Biljana Plavsic created the unit. Now she was president up until 1998. So my question is: Under whose authority or who was your superior for the time that you had your unit protecting General Mladic while he was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: My superior command was the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. According to the then-rules of the military police, this unit was subordinated to the chief of General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and professionally it was the chief of the Security Administration that was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that that is the case up until 2001, when you no longer -- when you ceased to function in this capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's the way it was until 2001, when my function ceased to exist. But how it was after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now there's been a lot of discussion about international arrest warrants, warrants issued nationally. I want to boil it down to an essential question: Isn't it true that you were not prepared to act solely on the -- an international arrest warrant issued by this court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not prepared to act because the organs in charge in my country did not ask me to do that. It wouldn't be clear to me what it is that I'm supposed to do. The authorities of my country appoint me to do such and such a job, and the international authorities are asking for something completely different. I would have been in a major dilemma, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You now have just said that the authorities in your country were asking to you do something completely different than the international authorities. What precisely was your understanding of what you -- the authorities of your country were asking you to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that the authorities asked me to have this unit secure the war command post and provide security for General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we started this discussion with paragraph 26 of your statement. I want to return to that. You say in relation to the Law on Co-operation with the ICTY: "The relevant law was adopted in June 2001 when I was no longer involved in securing the general." My question to you is: Is it true that after you left you no longer had anything to do with securing General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I had nothing to do with securing General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that includes not only in an official capacity but in an unofficial capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I had nothing to do with providing security for General Mladic in an official capacity. And as for an unofficial capacity, I had no need for that to deal with his security, and I did not deal with his security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that in 2003 the European Union placed a travel ban on you because it had information that you were part of a network providing support to indicted war criminals, including General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I admit that that is what the European community did, but I do not admit that I did anything in respect of the security of General Mladic after I left that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that in 2003 the United States also placed a travel ban on you for the same reasons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for the same reason. But I'm saying once again this was based on their information up until 2001 when I was there. After 2001, February 2001, I did not take part in General Mladic's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that on the 29th of May, 2003, you were placed on a list of the USA Office of Foreign Assets which restricted your ability to conduct international financial transactions because it believed that you were part of a network that was supporting war criminals. Do you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I acknowledge that. But I was not part of that network that gave this support, but I do acknowledge that this had been done by the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that on the 7th of July, 2003, the Office of the High Representative in Bosnia placed a freeze on your bank accounts in Bosnia because of information it had that you were part of a network that was supporting war criminals. Do you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I acknowledge that too. But I was not part of this network, as they had put it. But I acknowledge that that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now all of these restrictions on your travel and finances, they remained in effect until General Mladic was captured; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know until that was -- well, what they based that I mean. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When were they lifted. When were you able to travel again, when were your bank accounts able to be accessed again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I had no bank accounts anyway. And I mean, these bans were lifted a few years ago, as far as I know. I don't know the exact year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you deny that you gave assistance to war criminals. Do you acknowledge that someone who helps hide a person -- well, do you acknowledge that someone who helps hide a person that has been indicted by this Tribunal -- I'm sorry, strike all of that. You've denied giving assistance to war criminals. Do you acknowledge that providing financial assistance to someone who is a fugitive is in fact rendering assistance to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I accept that. Whoever this gives that kind of assistance, yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the 8th of July 2004 SFOR soldiers as well as police executed a search warrant on your apartment in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That was not my apartment. That was the apartment of Colonel Jovan Lalovic. And SFOR missed on that score. It was the apartment of Colonel Jovan Lalovic and they were looking for General Lalovic in that apartment. That was not my apartment. SFOR never searched a single apartment of mine or any place where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 25 of your statement, you talk about being relieved of duty and you say: "On 11 July 2003, the SFOR commander relieved me of the above duty because I allegedly assisted General Ratko Mladic in his hiding. That was certainly not true." Have I read that correctly? Have you characterised your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: You paraphrased my words correctly. It is correct that the commander of SFOR replaced me, but I'm saying that it's not true that I helped General Ratko Mladic hide because while I was commander of the security unit the General was not hiding. You already asked me about that, and we talked about the apartment and the facilities where he stayed from time to time. He moved about Belgrade like any other citizen. He went to the market-place to shop. He went to stores to buy bread. He went to football games.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: He met in different places with some of his -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll all doing our best to try to allow you to catch your plane today, so if you can please be brief in your answers to me, it would be appreciated. While General Mladic was a fugitive did you ever authorise payments be made to him? I saw you nod your head but I didn't hear an answer. Did you ever authorise payments to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I did not authorise any payments to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever order your subordinates to process payments for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now while he was a fugitive, my office undertook efforts to locate him. The national authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina also undertook efforts. As part of their efforts, they undertook a series of interviews. I want to deal with things three different people said about you in their statements to the Ministry of Security of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Each of these three people came into knowledge that you were instrumental in assisting Mladic. Person number one was one of the people who processed payments to the VRS and VJ members. He saw Ratko Mladic was being paid and questioned it. He said that an authorised officer would verify the payment list and it usually was Colonel Dragan Lalovic. Do you accept that person 1 is referring to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: If this person is mentioning Colonel Dragan Lalovic, then this person is referring to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Person 2 said that when he saw Ratko Mladic's name on a payment list for a unit that he knew Mladic did not belong to that he went to Colonel Dragan Lalovic and told him that he would not process the paperwork without someone's order. He said you told him that you had been ordered to process the payment and you were, in turn, ordering him. Do you accept that person number 2 is referring to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Person number 2 is referring to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you accept what person number 2 says as being truthful?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I have to explain that to you. The payment of officers is carried out on the basis of appointment orders and on the basis of the report on handing over duty. The appointment decision is made by the authority in charge, and the report on the hand-over of duty is compiled by the personnel organ who then gives it to the person involved, and then that person signs it and then the so-called work lists are written up. A work list is a document, including the names of all the persons who serve in that military post, and the work list is signed by the commander. I sign it. With my signature, I just verify that these persons were at work. I am not the person that is issuing payments to them, that is giving them money. Salaries and money, that is what their officers, their superiors, make possible. In the case of General Mladic, it is probably the General Staff or the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During what period of time did you sign payment lists on which you saw General Mladic's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Then when I was commander of the unit. Before that, that was done by Colonel Beara. When Beara left, then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me quoting is person 2 also said. "It is important to mention that the name of Ratko Mladic, without any rank, was on internal lists which was logged for the unit command, which was at the end of the month, each month, given to me by Colonel Dragan Lalovic." Again, do you accept that this is a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I accept that this is a reference to me, but then there was also a reference to rank. And all these lists that I signed were sent to the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka to the organ in charge of exercising control so then this organ could also intervene. If somebody was not supposed to be on this list, they could intervene and say such and such a person should not be on that list. Nobody intervened. Nobody wanted to have General Mladic removed from that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if you had not signed those lists, would the payment have gone through to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Had I not signed these lists, somebody else would have signed them and he would have certainly have received that. And if I wouldn't have received it, it wasn't only General Mladic who would not have received his salary, nobody from the unit would have received his salary, you see? Actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: -- it was not a salary. It was a compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- a few minutes ago when I asked you did you ever authorise payments to General Mladic? "A. No, no." Is that answer true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I signed this, that General Mladic was present in the unit. That does not mean that I approved the payment. That's what I mean. Somebody else is approving the payment. Had General Mladic not had an order on appointment, I could have signed this list who knows how many times, but he never would have received it had he not had an appointment decision. That is why I stated what I stated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Person 3 gave information that payments for Mladic were collected for him by officers stationed at Topcider barracks. Would these officers likely be your subordinates which you referred to earlier as being billeted at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who collected it. If that's true, I suppose it was his secretary or somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: These were soldiers that collected the -- his payments. Let me just tell you something else person number 3 said: "I don't know if the above described method of paying salaries was regulated in some rule-book. I did it by the oral order of Unit Commander Dragan Lalovic." Do you accept that person number 3 is referring to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is referring to me. But that is regulated by the rule-book. It could not have been done on my verbal order. Everybody knows how salaries and compensation sayings are received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that you gave an oral order for payments to be made to General Mladic at the time he was a fugitive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object. It's asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you accept the truth of what person number 3 has said about receiving an oral order from you to pay -- make a payment to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: What person 3 said is not true. It's not true that I verbally decided how compensation would be given to General Mladic. I couldn't have done that. It's governed by rules and regulations, how salaries are paid out and how they are received. That person is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the name of Drazen Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Drazen Milovanovic? No. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name of Dragan Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, you have to explain who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Both of these men were young soldiers guarding an underground shelter in Topcider. On the 5th of October, 2004, both were killed. A military commission headed by Vuk Tufegdzic investigated the killings and said that Jakovljevic killed Milovanovic and then committed suicide. Do you now recall who these two men were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I remember what you're talking about, but I heard it from media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A second investigation was carried out by the High Council of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Groome. You were earlier asked do you recognise the name of Drazen Milovanovic. You said Drazen Milovanovic? No, I can't remember. Do you recognise the name of Dragan Jakovljevic? No. No, you have to explain who they are. And two minutes later you say yes, I read these names in the media. I heard from media reports. I remember what you're talking about but I heard from media reports. And they were so extensive, weren't they, these media reports? Weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the gentleman asked me for the first time about these name, I really couldn't remember. But when he started telling the story about the Topcider barracks, I remembered the cause because I learned from media reports what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being so close to what your previous job was, nothing didn't ring a bell at all you heard these names? Where even I, as newspaper reader, have read about that story so many times, including names. And you, so close to your previous job, had no idea about these names? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sir, I don't know -- I don't know what I have to do with these people and how am I supposed to remember their names? By that time, I had been retired for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that it was nothing of special interest to you, even not in relation to your previous job, if I understand you well? Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A second investigation was carried out by the High Council of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro headed by Bozidar Prelevic. The investigation concluded that both men were murdered by a third person. Now the parents of these two young soldiers have repeatedly stated their belief that their sons were murdered on a military base in Topcider because they inadvertently learned that Mladic was hiding there. In an interview in 2013 to Balkan Insight, the father of Dragan Jakovljevic told them: "'A month ago we got a letter signed by the former security of the ICTY indictee, in which it was described what happened that day. The letter says that Mladic was present that day in the barracks and that our two boys noticed him,' said Janko Jakovljevic, the father of one of the dead soldiers in July last year. Jakovljevic said that Mladic requested that the two soldiers be killed." As a former member of Mladic's security team who is at this time still on lists because it was believed that you were still participating in sheltering him, were you also aware that the soldiers were ordered to be killed because they found out that Mladic was hiding at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know that installation at Topcider existed until that happened, until this happened. That's one. And, second, I had been retired by that time for a long time. I have nothing do with it, and I can't believe it is as you represent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Lukic, that Mr. Mladic wanted to consult one counsel. No, no, we're not taking a break. You may consult with counsel, write a little note, or we'll continue with the examination. And switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic you remain -- Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could you please remove Mr. Mladic from the courtroom. Mr. Mladic should be removed from the courtroom immediately. We go into closed session. We go into closed session. Mr. Mladic is to be removed from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours I'll conclude my questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll conclude your questions. Mr. Lukic, any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just several questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are a little bit going beyond the time, but I take it that there was such an urgent request for the witness to be able to leave, I see nodding yes from the booth. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend Groome was trying to clarify something with you but I don't believe it has been cleared up completely. In your opinion, both in the FRY and in Republika Srpska, when did it become illegal to help or guard Ratko Mladic? Let me try to help you -- let me try to read what you said. Page 74, line 13 it reads -- I will be reading in English and you will receive interpretation. [In English] "As far as I know, General Mladic became a wanted man in Republika Srpska in May 2000, roughly at that time in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ..." [Interpretation] I'm only interested if the year is correct here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 2001. If I said 2000 earlier, then it was a slip of the tongue. In fact, wait a moment. 2002. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: After so many dates and years, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to finish this quickly. You know that the president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Sarovic was relieved of duty because he was expecting of helping General Mladic. Do you know that he is now conducting proceedings, a lawsuit because he had managed to prove that he not been assisting General Mladic. He is suing for damages.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was wrongly accused, but I didn't know about this lawsuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what kind of proceedings was it established that you were helping Mladic so that bans were placed on your travel, finances, et cetera? Were you informed of these proceedings and were you a party to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about it. Nothing was explained to me. It was only said to me that these measures were being applied against me because I am suspected of assisting war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding these payments, did you have the right to abolish somebody's acquired right and right to a salary or compensation or to institute somebody's right to receive salary when you were signing these lists on which Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. I only said that I was signing those lists, and the lists were only proof that somebody was present at work at that time on that day or that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the legal proceedings involving the murders of these two soldiers at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm only following media reports, if this is what you want me to say here, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Do you know that in those proceedings General Mladic was heard here in The Hague as a witness, not as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, General, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one short question for you. Earlier we looked at the statement of Mr. Milovanovic. You refer that was about access to the archives and you remember that document, that statement, which is P6549. Now, in the beginning of that -- a little bit higher up on the same page, which is on -- and I'll read it for you, which is page 268 in English, General Milovanovic stated the following. "General Mladic and I put ourselves at the disposal of the VRS for up to six months and for the other six months to the Yugoslav army. General Mladic stayed in Crna Rijeka with his security guards who were supposed to protect him from being arrested by The Hague Tribunal. Biljana Plavsic signed a decree about this. In the beginning, the commander of that powerful security, or security group, was Colonel Ljubisa Beara because Mladic wished it so, and then it was Colonel, and later General, Dragan Lalovic also because Mladic wished it so."
